citation: Wightman MA, Vaughan RW. Comparison of Compounds Used for Intradermal Anesthesia. Anesthesiology 1976;45(6):687-689
text_quality: ocr — the PDF is a scan with no text layer and no OCR engine is installed in this session, so texts/S-686-39.txt is a manual transcription from the three page images in texts/scans/. Body text, both figure legends and all ten references are transcribed; the two figures are charts, and the per-timepoint values exist only as plotted points, so figure values are described rather than read off as numbers.
design: Randomised, double-blind, within-subject comparison; volunteers served as their own controls. Two-way ANOVA by subject and drug, then subject-adjusted one-way ANOVA with a priori and a posteriori contrasts.
population: 20 adult volunteers, 16 men and 4 women, aged 19 to 45 years, ASA physical status 1, none taking analgesics, sedatives or tranquilizers. Human Studies Committee approval.
n: 20 subjects, each receiving all six solutions (six wheals per subject, three per hand); n = 20 observations per solution
setting: Department of Anesthesiology, University of Arizona School of Medicine, Tucson; subjects seated, dorsum of each hand
intervention: Six single-dose solutions given as intradermal wheals: physiologic saline; saline with benzyl alcohol; lidocaine at a lower strength; lidocaine at that same lower strength with methylparaben; lidocaine at a higher strength; and procaine. Water was the diluent for the local anaesthetics and no other additive was present. [dose figures omitted]
comparator: Each solution against the other five within the same subject; physiologic saline alone served as the inactive comparator
route: Intradermal wheal, dorsum of the hand, 25-gauge needle, order of injections randomised, subjects did not observe the injections
duration: Anaesthesia assessed by pin prick from 15 seconds after injection at intervals to a total observation window of 20 minutes. The window bounds the study: it does not time recovery to completion for the lidocaine arms, which were still anaesthetic when observation stopped.
outcomes: (1) Discomfort on injection, rated 0 (no discomfort) to 2 (severe discomfort); (2) degree of anaesthesia by pin prick, rated 0 (no anaesthesia) to 3 (excellent anaesthesia), plotted against time; (3) adverse local effects at injection sites

key_results.quote: A randomized, double-blind study was carried out with 20 adult volunteers serving as their own controls
Anesthesia produced by the wheal of intradermal drug was tested by pin prick, initially 15 seconds after injection and at intervals thereafter to a total duration of 20 minutes.
Methylparaben did not alter the duration or intensity of anesthesia.
Satisfactory anesthesia began to dissipate after 2 to 3 minutes with benzyl alcohol-saline solution, after 5 minutes with procaine, and after 20 minutes with the lidocaine preparations
Methylparaben preservative in lidocaine multidose vials did not alter the incidence of discomfort.
Injection of physiologic saline solution alone caused the greatest discomfort.
The duration of anesthesia with lidocaine exceeded that produced by procaine, but both far exceeded the few minutes needed in most situations in clinical anesthesia.
Reactions, consisting of localized itching, erythema, and pseudopod formation, appeared in eight of 20 subjects given procaine, but in no other subject.
Physiologic saline solution alone causes severe pain on injection and provides no anesthesia, despite claims to the contrary.

funding_conflicts: None stated. Departmental affiliation only (Department of Anesthesiology, University of Arizona School of Medicine). No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the paper, which is normal for a 1976 clinical report.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Mark LC. Letter to the editor. N Engl J Med 1976;294:614
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: the source of the claim that physiologic saline is a satisfactory discomfort-free local anaesthetic; Wightman tests and rejects it, which bears on any page claim that saline wheals anaesthetise

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: the origin of benzyl alcohol as an infiltration anaesthetic; bears on claims about preservative vehicles having anaesthetic activity of their own

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: cited for local tissue damage from high benzyl alcohol concentrations in oil; bears on vehicle-related tissue-injury claims

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: cited for severe local hypersensitivity to methylparaben; bears on claims about preservative-driven reactions being mistaken for lidocaine allergy
